item.content:encoded:
At Glasgow last month, Pacific island nations won ten Commonwealth Games medals. Six of them came in weightlifting. Two in boxing, one in judo, one in lawn bowls. On the track, not a single Pacific runner got past the first round of the men’s 400 or 800 metres.

Fiji took two of those medals – a weightlifting gold to Taniela Rainibogi and a boxing bronze to Jasmine Daunakamakama, our first female Commonwealth boxing medal. Both deserve every bit of the celebration they received.

But look at the shape of that list rather than the total. We win where a narrow, focused pathway has been built around a small number of athletes. We disappear entirely from the events that need a broad development pipeline underneath them. That is not a statement about our athletes. It is a statement about what sits behind them.

And the usual explanation – that we are a small country and we cannot afford to compete – does not survive contact with the budget.

The Ministry of Youth and Sports was allocated $F23.4 million for 2025–2026. Inside that figure sit some revealing lines: about $F5.4m for overseas sporting tours, $F3.9m for hosting international tournaments, $F1.9m for engaging coaches, and $F670,000 for the Fiji Sports Council.

Now consider Jamaica. A country of 2.8 million people – three times our population – grant-funds every one of its national sporting associations through a foundation running on roughly $US4.5m a year. And Jamaica is a sprinting superpower.

The two figures are not a perfect comparison. A whole ministry vote is a different instrument from a grant-making foundation. But the orders of magnitude are the point: Fiji’s sports allocation, serving fewer than a million people, is not obviously smaller per head than Jamaica’s, and on some lines, it is plainly larger.

A country that can find $F5.4m for tours and $F3.9m to host tournaments cannot honestly say poverty is the reason its development pipeline runs dry.

So if the money is appropriated, where does it go?

The first problem is execution. In 2024–25, the Ministry of Youth and Sports had a revised allocation of $F23.42m and spent F$21.85m. Against a revised capital provision of $F1.83m – the money that builds and improves sporting infrastructure – actual capital spending was only $F589,500. Less than a third. The gap between what is budgeted and what reaches the ground is itself a failure of conversion.

The second is leakage, and it is not only governmental. Within the federations and apex bodies that receive the grants, money intended for athletes too often does not reach them. FASANOC itself has said it is unacceptable that some federations, rather than meeting their share of costs, have pushed the burden back onto the athletes they exist to serve.

Read those two facts together and the picture is not scarcity. It is conversion. We are not failing to fund sport. We are failing to turn funding into coaching, competition and pathways.

Here is what should make this frustrating rather than depressing: the expensive, difficult thing is already built.

Every year, the Coca-Cola Games fill a stadium. Tens of thousands of Fijians watch schoolchildren compete at a level of intensity that most countries would envy. Jamaica has an equivalent – their inter-school championships, known simply as Champs – and it is the foundation of their sprinting dominance.

The difference is not the schools’ competition. We match them there. The difference is what sits above it. Champs feeds a deliberate high-performance pathway: coaching, progression, selection, funding, a route from a school carnival to a world final. Ours largely stops at the spectacle. We stage a magnificent talent identification exercise every year and then, for most of those children, nothing follows.

In 2018, a young lifter from Levuka won gold at the Commonwealth Games – Fiji’s only gold of those Games. Her name is Eileen Cikamatana. After a falling-out with the sport’s administration here, she transferred her allegiance to Australia in 2019.

She has won Commonwealth gold for Australia ever since. At Birmingham she became the first woman to win individual Commonwealth golds for two different countries. At Glasgow last month she won a third consecutive title.

This is not a story about money. No professional league lured her away; weightlifting has no riches to offer. Rugby players who leave for Australia, New Zealand and France are responding to careers that genuinely do not exist here, and no one can blame them for that. It is a pull, and answering it takes money and professional structures we may not have.

What happened to Cikamatana was a push. And a push costs nothing to prevent. It asks only that our federations govern themselves decently, keep faith with the coaches who develop athletes, and treat the people they exist to serve as human beings rather than assets to be administered.

At Glasgow, Fiji celebrated a weightlifting gold while a woman from Levuka stood on another country’s podium. Both of those achievements began here. Only one of them was still ours.

We usually answer all of this by pointing to rugby sevens, and we are entitled to. But we should read it honestly.

Sevens did not begin as something we built. It began as something we had – a vast reservoir of informal play, village and provincial tournaments, schools competition, producing exactly the raw material the short game rewards. The professional structure came late and largely harvested an advantage that was already there. It converted the gift; it did not create it.

And that gift is now being closed down. As Argentina, Spain and others professionalise sevens deliberately, the premium on raw Fijian flair compresses. Our endowment has not shrunk. The field has organised around it – and organisation is precisely the thing we have leaned on least.

None of this is a criticism of our athletes. The talent has never been the constraint — it is the one thing we have never been short of. Our players succeed the moment they step inside somebody else’s functioning system, which tells you exactly where the problem lies.

Change what stands behind the scoreboard, and the scoreboard will change.

The Coca-Cola Games: Fiji already has the schools competition. What is missing is the pathway above it. Picture: FIJI TIMES FILE

Taniela Tuisuva Rainibogi of Fiji is presented the Gold medal during the medal ceremony for the Men’s 110kg Weightlifting during the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games at the SEC Armadillo in Glasgow, Scotland on July 30, 2026. Picture: AAP/LUKAS COCH

item.title: Economic catalyst | Innovation hub to power next generation of startups
item.description: THE Reserve Bank of Fiji (RBF) has unveiled the new Fiji Innovation Hub space at the central bank’s building in Suva in a move to strengthen the country’s innovation ecosystem and the next generation of entrepreneurs and startups. The new hub will provide a central platform where innovators, startups, development partners and industry stakeholders can connect, collaborate, and access needed suppor
item.content:encoded:
THE Reserve Bank of Fiji (RBF) has unveiled the new Fiji Innovation Hub space at the central bank’s building in Suva in a move to strengthen the country’s innovation ecosystem and the next generation of entrepreneurs and startups.

The new hub will provide a central platform where innovators, startups, development partners and industry stakeholders can connect, collaborate, and access needed support to transform ideas into scalable solutions.

RBF governor Ariff Ali said the creation of a dedicated environment was a significant move where innovation could thrive, and entrepreneurs could access the support needed to turn ideas into impactful solutions.

“Innovation is no longer a peripheral issue. It is central to Fiji’s economic future,” Mr Ali said in his address.

“This space will serve as a hub for innovation, driving economic opportunities and providing a platform to leverage technology in addressing Fiji’s economic challenges.”

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Industries, Commerce, Business Development and Public Enterprises Manoa Kamikamica officiated at the event, and reiterated the Government’s commitment to fostering innovation as a driver of economic resilience, productivity and competitiveness.

“The Fiji Innovation Hub serves as a catalyst for driving this agenda forward and fostering sustainable economic growth,” Mr Kamikamica said.

Ambassador of the European Union to the Pacific Barbara Plinkert said: “Fiji Innovation Hub brings elements that the global gateway activities and the learnings from the EU-Pacific Business Forum have echoed – connectivity, digital transformation, resilience and sustainable economic development.”

The event also recognised the contributions of the Fiji Innovation Hub’s partners who were instrumental in establishing the hub’s new premises and advancing its successful pilot year.

The launch brought together representatives from Government, development partners, the private sector, financial institutions and the entrepreneurial community to celebrate the opening of a facility that will serve as a catalyst for innovation, enterprise development and economic opportunity.

During the event, Mr Kamikamica also announced the addition of two new partners – the Ministry of Policing and Communications, and the Fiji Development Bank that have committed to provide sponsorship support for the Fiji Innovation Hub’s second year activities.

item.title: Fiji commissions first eco-friendly electric ambulift
item.description: Fiji Airports has commissioned its first state-of-the-art fully electric ambulift at the Nadi International Airport. Funded through the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the Japanese government, the ambulift is anticipated to strengthen the airport manager’s commitment to operational excellence and an inclusive travel experience for all passengers.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji Airports has commissioned its first state-of-the-art fully electric ambulift at the Nadi International Airport.

Funded through the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the Japanese government, the ambulift is anticipated to strengthen the airport manager’s commitment to operational excellence and an inclusive travel experience for all passengers.

The ambulift is designed to safely board and disembark persons with reduced mobility and passengers requiring additional assistance.

Fiji Airport chief executive officer Mesake Nawari said the ambulift commissioning reflected their focus on improving passenger experience through inclusive and sustainable infrastructure.

“This commissioning represents far more than the introduction of new equipment,” Mr Nawari said. “It is about ensuring that every passenger can travel through our airport safely, comfortably and with dignity. The new electric ambulift will strengthen accessibility while also supporting our transition towards cleaner airport operations.”

He said they were building airport facilities that were more inclusive, efficient and prepared for the future needs of Fiji and the wider Pacific.

“As our first fully electric operational vehicle on the airside, the ambulift provides a strong foundation for introducing more sustainable equipment and vehicles as we continue implementing the Fiji Airports Master Plan and progress towards our Net Zero carbon emission target for scopes 1 and 2 by 2030.”

ADB regional director Azusa Sato said the investment demonstrated their commitment to supporting inclusive, resilient and sustainable infrastructure in Fiji and across the Pacific – in partnership with the Japanese government and Fiji Airports.

Japanese ambassador to Fiji Hiroshi Tajima said Japan was pleased to support an initiative that would directly improve accessibility and service delivery for passengers.

“As air travel and tourism continue to grow across the Pacific, ensuring accessibility for all travellers is becoming increasingly important,” Mr Tajima said in a statement from Fiji Airports.

The ambulift will be operated by six specially trained Fiji Airports drivers who have completed specialised operational training delivered by technical experts from China.

The commissioning event also featured demonstrations of a new walk-through metal detector and passenger screening equipment at the primary screening point, which will further strengthen aviation security and support more efficient passenger processing at the Nadi International Airport.

item.title: Discounted pricing secured under MoU
item.description: More than 10,000 farmers from various commodity organisations registered with the Fiji Crop and Livestock Council (FCLC) will soon benefit from a new memorandum of understanding (MoU) that aims to discount prices of equipment to farmers. The agreement was signed between the FCLC and Ba Industries Limited, one of the country’s largest distributors of agri-products and farming equipment.
item.content:encoded:
More than 10,000 farmers from various commodity organisations registered with the Fiji Crop and Livestock Council (FCLC) will soon benefit from a new memorandum of understanding (MoU) that aims to discount prices of equipment to farmers.

The agreement was signed between the FCLC and Ba Industries Limited, one of the country’s largest distributors of agri-products and farming equipment.

Under the agreement, registered farmers and are financial members of respective commodity organisations will access the FCLC Farmers Loyalty Programme, translating into significant savings on agricultural inputs and equipment.

FCLC chief executive officer Jiu Daunivalu said said the MoU with Ba Industries Ltd meant farmers would access real, tangible savings through the loyalty program.

“We welcome the support of business partners like Ba Industries, who bring not only their expertise in agriculture but also help put the right tools in farmers’ hands at a discount.”

Ba Industries representative Atin Patel said under the partnership, the company would provide training and support services on the use and maintenance of its products.

“We see our AgriTech brand as a way forward, helping farmers use knowledge and technology to build a career in farming, which delivers financial benefits to them and to the nation,” Mr Patel said in a statement from the FCLC.

Ms Daunivalu said the partnership reflected their core mandate to grow the business of agriculture in Fiji.

“For the past 10 years, through FCLC’s programs, we have seen what’s possible when farmers are given the right training and the right support, especially in understanding markets and business planning,” she said.

“This changes mindsets and farming practices as farmers realise they are building careers, and sustainable, profitable businesses.

“I’m glad to see this new drive toward commercialisation and modernisation coming from the farmers themselves.

“A memorandum of understanding with a reputable, well-established company like Ba Industries is a practical, everyday mechanism for doing exactly that.”

item.title: Education Minister Radrodro rejects NFP claims
item.description: Education Minister Aseri Radrodro has rejected claims by the National Federation Party that he misrepresented the Electoral Act over the use of school premises for political campaigning. “I was approached by The Fiji Times journalist to respond to questions on the use of school premises for political rallies,” Radrodro said.
item.content:encoded:
Education Minister Aseri Radrodro has rejected claims by the National Federation Party that he misrepresented the Electoral Act over the use of school premises for political campaigning.

“I was approached by The Fiji Times journalist to respond to questions on the use of school premises for political rallies,” Radrodro said.

“I had responded that there are MOE policies that any use of school premises need to be on the consent of the Permanent Secretary for Education.”

His comments follow a statement from NFP general secretary Kamal Iyer, who accused the Minister of misrepresenting section 113 and imposing restrictions on community and organisation-owned school halls.

The Minister instead pointed to section 150(c) of the Electoral Act, which he said specifically deals with campaigning at educational institutions.

He quoted the provision as stating that any person who conducts a campaign on the premises of an educational institution commits an offence and is liable upon conviction to a fine of up to $10,000, imprisonment for up to five years, or both.

“Until section 150 of the Fiji Electoral Act 2014 is amended or revised, it is the law at present,” Radrodro said.

He maintained that the Ministry of Education would protect the political neutrality of schools and ensure their premises were not used for political campaigning by any party.

Radrodro said the Ministry also had a responsibility to protect the integrity of educational institutions and the wellbeing of students and teachers.

He said all political parties must respect the law and “operate on an equal footing under Fiji’s electoral laws.”

item.title: One Nation declares no assets or liabilities, lists $5,005 in contributions
item.description: The One Nation political party has declared no assets or liabilities while reporting $5,005 in contributions received, according to its declaration of assets, liabilities, income and expenditure. The declaration was made pursuant to sections 16(2) and 16(3) of the Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding & Disclosures) Act 2013.
item.content:encoded:
The One Nation political party has declared no assets or liabilities while reporting $5,005 in contributions received, according to its declaration of assets, liabilities, income and expenditure.

The declaration was made pursuant to sections 16(2) and 16(3) of the Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding & Disclosures) Act 2013.

Under its declaration of assets and liabilities, the party recorded nil total assets and nil total liabilities.

The declaration also states that One Nation does not currently have a bank account, with the party indicating it was in the process of opening one and would provide the account details to the Registrar in accordance with the requirements of the Act.

Under contributions, donations and pledges, the party declared $5,005 in contributions or donations received, with no contributions or donations received in kind and no pledges recorded.

The four individual contributions making up the $5,005 total came from Faiyaz Koya ($1,250), Viam Pillay ($1,250), Sanjay Kirpal ($1,255) and Ketan Lal ($1,250).

The declaration also contains figures for the party’s income and expenditure during the reporting period.

The document forms part of the financial disclosure requirements imposed on registered political parties under Fiji’s political parties legislation.

item.title: Heavy rain alert remains in force for parts of Fiji
item.description: A heavy rain alert remains in force for Viti Levu, Yasawa, Mamanuca, Kadavu and nearby smaller islands, with isolated heavy falls and thunderstorms forecast today. The National Weather Forecasting Centre in Nadi, in its 5.30am bulletin today, said a trough of low pressure continues to affect the western part of the country.
item.content:encoded:
A heavy rain alert remains in force for Viti Levu, Yasawa, Mamanuca, Kadavu and nearby smaller islands, with isolated heavy falls and thunderstorms forecast today.

The National Weather Forecasting Centre in Nadi, in its 5.30am bulletin today, said a trough of low pressure continues to affect the western part of the country.

Occasional rain, isolated heavy falls and thunderstorms are forecast over Viti Levu, Yasawa, Mamanuca, Kadavu and nearby smaller islands through to midnight tonight.

Cloudy periods with some showers are expected elsewhere.

Moderate to fresh easterly winds are forecast, while seas are expected to be moderate to rough.

Similar conditions are expected to continue into Tuesday, with occasional rain, isolated heavy falls and thunderstorms again forecast for Viti Levu, Yasawa, Mamanuca, Kadavu and nearby smaller islands.

Cloudy periods with some showers are expected elsewhere on Tuesday.

item.title: Seruiratu questions TRC powers, demands results from $1.5M allocation
item.description: Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu has questioned whether Fiji’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission has been given sufficient powers to uncover the full truth behind the political upheavals of 1987, 2000 and 2006. Seruiratu says almost two years into the process, fundamental questions remain unanswered about the individuals who planned, supported, financed or influenced Fiji’s coups.
item.content:encoded:
Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu has questioned whether Fiji’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission has been given sufficient powers to uncover the full truth behind the political upheavals of 1987, 2000 and 2006.

Seruiratu says almost two years into the process, fundamental questions remain unanswered about the individuals who planned, supported, financed or influenced Fiji’s coups.

“I raised this concern in Parliament last December when I asked: Who were the people behind 1987? and who were the people behind 2000?” Seruiratu said.

He acknowledged the importance of the Commission hearing from victims and families but argued that documenting their experiences alone would not establish the full circumstances behind Fiji’s political crises.

“Recording people’s suffering is not, by itself, the same as establishing the truth about why these events happened, who planned them, who supported them and who benefited from them,” he said.

Seruiratu’s central concern is that the Commission does not have the power to summon witnesses.

He questioned how it could establish the truth if people with critical information refused to voluntarily appear.

“Government cannot establish a Commission to find the truth and then deny that Commission the power to require those who may hold that truth to appear before it,” he said.

Seruiratu also questioned the Government’s allocation of another $1.5 million to the Commission in the 2026–2027 National Budget, saying taxpayers were entitled to expect measurable results.

“The Opposition does not object to spending money on a credible process that can establish the truth and contribute towards lasting national reconciliation,” he said.

“What we question is spending another $1.5 million on a Commission that Government itself has prevented from using one of the most important tools available to uncover that truth.”

Seruiratu said the Commission should ultimately provide answers about who was involved in Fiji’s political upheavals, what occurred behind the scenes and what lessons could prevent similar events in the future.

He also pointed to Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka’s appearance before the Commission, saying Rabuka had stated that he succumbed to pressure from influential figures in carrying out the 1987 coup.

“The obvious question is: who were those influential figures?” Seruiratu said.

“The Commission should have the ability to pursue that evidence. It should be able to identify those individuals, summon relevant witnesses, examine their evidence and establish what role, if any, they played.”

Seruiratu said George Speight, people with direct knowledge of the 2000 events, and former and serving RFMF officers with relevant information should be heard by the Commission.

He stressed that strengthening the Commission’s powers should not be about conducting a “witch-hunt” or using the process to prosecute individuals.

“The purpose should be to establish, as accurately as possible, what happened, who was involved, why it happened and how Fiji can prevent it from happening again,” he said.

Seruiratu called on the Government to explain what had been achieved with previous funding and what specific outcomes taxpayers could expect from the additional $1.5 million.

“If Government is serious about reconciliation, it must give the Commission the tools to find that truth,” he said.

“If taxpayers are expected to fund it, then Government must ensure that the country receives tangible results.”
